info.title: Hikube API
info.description:
Manage the resources of the Hikube platform.

## Errors

An error response carries an HTTP status for the class of the error and a JSON body (`ErrorResponse`) whose `code` identifies the precise error:

```json
{"requestId": "4bf92f3577b34da6a3ce929d0e0e4736", "code": 20101, "message": "invalid name: must be at least 3 characters", "details": []}
```

A code reads as a service prefix followed by three digits: `001`–`099` are platform errors (not found, already exists, unavailable…), `100`–`199` invalid input, `200`–`299` business rules. Handle errors on `code`: the wording of `message` may change.

### Common

|------|-------|
| 10001 | Authentication failed: invalid bearer token |
| 10002 | Permission denied: missing or invalid credentials, or credentials that do not allow this operation |
| 10003 | Event stream ticket expired |
| 10004 | The api-key could not be checked (temporary); retry, the key is not known to be invalid |
| 10005 | Refused by a platform admission policy; the message names the field, `details` the policy and its reason |
| 10006 | Invalid update_mask: a path names no updatable field, or one key of a collection |

put.description: Stops an unfinished backup run where the storage driver can stop, ending it failed with the message "Backup cancelled.". Works for a run not started yet, a Postgres backup still waiting to start, a VM instance or disk run (its data transfers are cancelled) and a MariaDB run. Refused with FailedPrecondition for a Postgres backup already running, a VM run that has not started moving data yet (retry in a few seconds), and a finished run. Deleting a run is not offered: the driver would carry on and leave an archive nothing refers to.

delete.description: Removes the record of a finished restore. Refused with FailedPrecondition while the restore is pending or running: the driver would carry on without a record, and the application would be released to a second restore. On a finished restore only the record goes; the application and the backup are unchanged. A VM restore that does not finish is stopped with CancelRestore.

BackupServiceCreateDestinationBody.description:
CreateDestinationRequest deliberately carries no endpoint, access-key or
secret-key field. Storage coordinates are derived from the referenced
bucket, and the way to guarantee a caller cannot supply them is for the
fields not to exist.

That invariant survives external storage rather than being traded away for
it: a destination will name a credential created through its own operation,
so the coordinates still never ride on this message.

The storage source is exactly one of the bucket pair or, later, a
credential. The fields are flat and the exclusivity is the validator's
(validateStorageSource), as the contract conventions require of exclusive
inputs: a oneof renders as unrelated optional properties in OpenAPI.

name.description: Plan name, unique within the project

cron.description: Five-field cron expression, or @hourly, @daily, @weekly, @monthly, @yearly, interpreted in UTC. Must not fire more than once per hour. @every and CRON_TZ=/TZ= prefixes are refused.

target.description:
Omit to restore over the backup's own source application. Naming that same
application explicitly is the identical operation and is treated as such.
Only postgres and mariadb accept a different target.

confirmDestructive.description: Required whenever the resolved target is the source application, or is an existing application that already holds data.

recoveryTime.description:
Postgres only. Must fall inside the backup's recovery_window: at or after
earliest, before last_commit_at and before cross_timeline_after. Omit it to
restore the state restore_point names. Exclusive with restore_point latest.

originalDisks.description: What becomes of the disks a VM instance restored over its source displaces. Either way they are replaced by the backup's copies. discard, the default, which empty means: what they held is deleted once the restore has succeeded, so a restore that says nothing does not start paying for a second copy; a restore that fails or is cancelled deletes nothing and keeps them as keep does, and its message says so. keep: what they held is kept as a disk of its own, named <disk>-orig-<id>, attached to nothing, listed and billed like any other disk. keep is refused on any other restore.

restorePoint.description: Postgres only, and only without recovery_time. backup, the default, which empty means: the state of the backup named. latest: the latest state its archived log reaches, along its history.

retentionDays.description: New retention in days. MariaDB, VM instance and VM disk archives keep the retention they were written with; Postgres archives are governed by the destination's current retention.

`NullValue` is a singleton enumeration to represent the null value for the
`Value` type union.

The JSON representation for `NullValue` is JSON `null`.

 - NULL_VALUE: Null value.

kind.description: Kind of the application: postgres, mariadb, instance (VM instance) or disk (VM disk). Required in a request. Empty in a response only for an application of a kind with no backup driver, which can exist only if created outside this API.

v1ApplicationRef.description:
ApplicationRef names an application inside the project. The API group is
always apps.cozystack.io and is therefore not part of the contract.

status.description: State of the stored archive. Always set. pending while it is being written; only ready can be restored from, and restorable says whether it still can.

location.description:
Archive URI. Never carries credentials. Empty for the VM kinds: their
data sits in a repository every VM backup of the destination shares, and
the driver's URI names only its own object in the platform's namespace.

sizeBytes.description:
Absent unless the driver measured it.

Cozystack v1.6.3 fills status.artifact.sizeBytes from its etcd strategy
alone; the cnpg, velero and mariadb strategies build an artifact carrying
the URI and nothing else, so none of the four kinds this API exposes
reports a size today. Absent rather than 0, because a zero that looks like
a measurement is worse than no answer — the same reasoning Cozystack's own
MariaDB controller applies when it leaves Artifact nil rather than set an
empty URI.

restorable.description:
Whether a restore from this backup would be admitted, as far as the API
can tell without reading the bucket: the backup is ready, a destination of
the name it was written to exists, is not being deleted, and was created
before the backup was taken — a destination created after it is another
one under the same name, and may point at another bucket. For the VM
kinds, the storage layer must also still hold the archive: Velero removes
it, data included, at the end of its retention, while this record stays.

It is not a check that the archive's objects are in the bucket. When
false, not_restorable_cause says which situation it is.

covers.description:
The other applications whose data this one archive also contains.

Backing up a VM instance captures the disks it runs on — the driver adds
one selector per disk, so a two-disk VM's archive holds both. Those disks
are applications in their own right, listed in the project's disks, and
until now nothing said they were backed up at all: an archive was findable
only under the application named in `application`.

This lists them rather than repeating the archive under each one. There is
one archive, written once, charged once, and `application` stays the single
answer to "what was this taken from" — a copy per disk would read as three
backups of three things.

It never names `application` itself, and it is empty for the kinds whose
archive holds one application's data and nothing else.

Listing by `application_name` matches on this too, which is the point: a
tenant asking what protects a disk gets the VM's archive back.

Being listed here is not being separately restorable. Restoring writes back
everything the archive covers, because the storage driver builds a
restore's scope from the backup rather than from the request — there is no
field on a restore that names a subset. A disk listed here is restored by
restoring the application in `application`, with its siblings.

recoveryWindow.description:
Postgres only: the span a point-in-time restore from this backup can
reach. Absent for every other kind, and for a Postgres backup whose base
backup end is not known. taken_at is when the base backup began, which is
earlier than any instant it can be restored to — see RecoveryWindow.

notRestorableReason.description:
Why restorable is false, in words that complete "this backup cannot be
restored because…". Empty when restorable is true. message stays the
driver's account of the backup itself.

notRestorableCause.description:
- not_ready: the backup is pending or failed.
  - destination_removed: no destination of that name exists. Only its
    record is known to be gone; whether the bucket still holds the data is
    not checked, and a destination recreated under that name does not
    bring the backup back (see destination_replaced).
  - destination_tearing_down: the destination's deletion has begun.
  - destination_replaced: a destination of that name exists but was
    created after the backup was taken, so it is not the one the backup
    was written to. This holds even when it points at the same bucket.
  - destination_unverified: the destinations could not be read; retry.
  - stored_archive_gone: VM kinds, the storage layer no longer holds the
    archive.

The source application having been deleted is not among them: the archive
is intact, and whether a restore needs another target is CreateRestore's
answer for the request it is given.

restorable is true. The situations call for different actions:

earliest.description:
The first instant from which a restore of this backup can be consistent,
and the instant restore_point backup aims at. PostgreSQL cannot stop
replaying before the backup it replays onto was consistent, so this — not
taken_at, which is when the base backup began — is the earliest instant
reachable. It is the end of the base backup as barman recorded it, or,
when a transaction written before the position the backup ended at is
stamped later than that, that transaction's time: aimed earlier, the
restore would stop before it reached consistency.

latest.description:
The last instant the archived log is known to cover, computed when the
backup is read: now, less the cluster's archive_timeout, less a minute for
the upload. An estimate on the safe side — the last archived segment is not
published by the platform, the forced-switch interval is. Re-read rather
than keep it: it moves forward with time, and it is not carried by events.

Absent when the database's continuous archiving is not working: then no
instant after the base backup can be promised, and a restore should not
name one.

Being inside the window is necessary, not sufficient. PostgreSQL stops at
the first transaction committed after the requested instant; on a
database that committed nothing since, it never finds one and the restore
fails. To get the latest state of an idle database, restore without a
recovery time.

lastCommitAt.description:
The last transaction — commit or abort — in the archived log this backup
replays through, read from the bucket, so it stays right when the source
is deleted or restored over. That log is the one PostgreSQL follows from
the backup's timeline: a transaction on another timeline of the same
stream does not count. A restore stops just before the first
transaction later than the instant asked for, so every instant at or after
this one fails, and is refused: the state it describes is the latest one,
which a restore without a recovery time gives.

With it known the reachable span is earliest up to, not including,
last_commit_at, and latest can be ignored. Absent with last_commit_known
false when the log could not be read; absent with last_commit_known true
when the replayed log holds no transaction at all. When it is earlier
than earliest, or absent with last_commit_known true, no instant is
reachable and only restore_point backup or latest works.

latestRestorable.description:
Whether restore_point latest replays this backup's history. False only
when it is established that it does not: the stream's most recent backup
lies on another timeline — a branch left by an earlier in-place restore
into the same stream — which is where CloudNativePG would start from.
True when the stream's backup catalog could not be read: CreateRestore
reads it again, and refuses then with 180221 if the branch is established,
or 180220 if the catalog still cannot be read.

crossTimelineAfter.description:
The first instant from which CloudNativePG would start from a backup on
another timeline, rather than one on this backup's history: instants at
or after it are refused (180221). Absent when none is established — no
such backup exists, which is the case of every stream with a single
history, or the catalog could not be read, in which case CreateRestore
reads it again and refuses an instant it still cannot place (180220).

v1TransferProgress.description:
TransferProgress reports how far a transfer has got.

It is present only for the VM kinds. Their data moves through Velero, which
measures it; the Postgres and MariaDB drivers hand the transfer to barman and
to a dump job, neither of which reports anything countable. The message is
therefore absent rather than zeroed for those kinds, so a client can tell
"no progress available for this kind" from "nothing transferred yet".

bytes_total is the volume read, not the space the archive occupies: Velero
deduplicates into a content-addressed repository, so the stored size is not a
per-backup quantity at all. Label it as data transferred, never as the size
of the backup.
